name: Rate with an Indefinite Denominator
pattern: quantity or frequency expression + NP[a(n) + singular unit nominal]

entry.name: Rate with an Indefinite Denominator
entry.pattern: quantity or frequency expression + NP[a(n) + singular unit nominal]

1.definition: Expresses a ratio by pairing a numerator with a unit denominator.
1.details: Fifty miles an hour supplies a speed, even if the measured motion lasts only a minute. Fifty miles every hour can instead assert successive hourly totals. The same form supports price, salary, and frequency. A per-phrase can often express the same ratio and is more flexible with stacked or complex denominators.

examples.form: He was going at [50 miles an hour].
The nurse checked it [twice a day].
examples.note: Constructed frequency example; the numerator can be multiplicative.

relatedConstructions.notes: The denominator is an indefinite singular NP.
Both combine with a stated magnitude, with different interpretations.

grounds.note: Compares the indefinite denominator with an every-time adjunct and a per-phrase.

projection.target: The second NP is interpreted as a unit denominator. The construction can describe a rate without asserting one complete occurrence of that unit.
projection.evidence: CGEL distinguishes the a- and per-forms. The FrameNet account controls the duration of motion in the comparison with every hour.

curious.title: Fifty miles an hour
curious.summary: Putting a or an before a unit, as in $20 a yard, turns an amount into a rate.
curious.body:
In He was going at 50 miles an hour, the words an hour don't mean one particular hour. They say what the 50 miles is measured against, so the whole phrase gives a speed. The same pattern gives a price, as in $20 a yard, and a frequency, as in twice a day.

The speed holds even if the trip lasts only a minute. Fifty miles every hour is different: it can claim fifty miles in each successive hour. A phrase with per can often say the same thing, and it copes better with longer or stacked units.

examples.text: He was going at [50 miles an hour].
The nurse checked it [twice a day].

curious.try: How would you say what a bicycle costs for each hour you rent it, using a and an hour or a day?

teacher.summary: Covers rates like fifty miles an hour, where a or an plus a unit expresses a ratio.
teacher.explain: The pattern pairs a quantity or frequency expression with a noun phrase made of a or an and a singular unit noun. It expresses a ratio: a numerator over a unit denominator. Fifty miles an hour gives a speed even if the motion lasts only a minute, whereas fifty miles every hour can assert successive hourly totals. The same form supports price, salary and frequency. The second noun phrase is interpreted as a unit denominator, and the construction describes a rate without asserting one complete occurrence of that unit. A per-phrase can often express the same ratio and is more flexible with stacked or complex denominators.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called a distributive use of a/an. The a/an here is the indefinite article in traditional terms, a determinative in CGEL terms.

examples.text: He was going at [50 miles an hour].
The nurse checked it [twice a day].

contrasts.text: He was going at 50 miles an hour.
contrasts.note: A rate, whatever the length of the trip.

watch_for: A learner might read an hour in fifty miles an hour as one particular hour.
A learner might assume the trip must last a whole hour for fifty miles an hour to be true.
teacher.activity: Students collect rates from signs, menus and timetables (price a kilo, trains an hour). They say each aloud with a or an, then restate it with per.

child.hook: How fast does a car go in "fifty miles an hour"?
child.explain: Sometimes a means "for each." Fifty miles an hour means fifty miles for each hour. A yard of ribbon at $20 a yard costs $20 for each yard.

examples.text: The car went [50 miles an hour].
The nurse checked it [twice a day].

child.play: Find prices and speeds on signs or packages. Say each one with a or an, such as three dollars a bag. Then say what it means with for each.
